name: William Tyndale
title: William Tyndale: the New Testament in the reader’s own language
description: Tyndale and the printing of the 1526 English New Testament: translation, persecution and an execution date that calls for caution.

sections.heading: The book that had to leave for another city
paragraphs: In 1525, William Tyndale was overseeing the printing of his translation of the New Testament in Cologne. The project was exposed and he had to leave the city. The surviving fragments of that printing remind us that the work moved forward amid scholarly labor, political risks and practical decisions.

In Worms, in 1526, the complete New Testament was printed in English. The Tyndale Society notes that it was the first in that language to be mass-produced on the printing press. There had been earlier English translations: Tyndale’s new contribution must be described precisely, with attention to his work from the Greek and to its spread in print.

sections.heading: Translating faithfully under pressure
paragraphs: Tyndale also worked from the Hebrew. The Pentateuch of his translation was published during his lifetime. His work took place amid religious controversy and opposition to the circulation of his books. He did not personally complete and publish an entire English Bible.

After his arrest, Tyndale was executed in 1536 near Brussels. The society devoted to his study cautions that October 6 is a traditional date, not a day established with documentary certainty. For that reason this story keeps the year and avoids turning the customary commemoration into an undisputed fact.

reflection: 2 Timothy 3:14–17 presents the Scriptures as a resource for teaching and shaping the believer’s life. Tyndale’s story helps us appreciate the work needed so that a reader can come to the text in his or her own language. Learning languages, checking terms and taking care over a printing are acts of service that often remain out of sight.

Access to the Bible also gives us a responsibility: to read attentively and humbly. The value of a translation depends on its faithfulness to the text, not on the fame of the one who produced it. Remembering Tyndale can stir up gratitude for those who translate and, at the same time, encourage us to compare, study and ask questions when a passage presents difficulties.
review_note: The “c.” is kept in the birth date. An execution on October 6 is not stated as a certain date, nor is it claimed that he produced the first English translation of any kind.
source_labels: Brian Buxton. “Tyndale’s translations and writings” (2013), The Tyndale Society.
